title: Short variable declaration
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Compares the two sides for equality
Declares a new variable
Assigns to an existing variable
explanation: Like let, but variables are mutable by default and there is no mut; := only works inside functions.

title: var declaration
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Declares an immutable total
Declares total, must be assigned before use
Declares total, initialized to 0
explanation: Go has no uninitialized variables: every type has a zero value, 0 for numbers, "" for strings, nil for pointers.

title: Constant
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A constant visible only inside the function below
A compile-time constant with no written type
A package-level variable, changeable at runtime
explanation: Constants may omit the type; an untyped constant takes whatever type the use site needs.

title: Function parameters
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: One tuple parameter
One int parameter; a has no type
Two parameters, both int
explanation: Types come after names, and adjacent parameters of the same type share one type; the result type follows the parentheses.

title: Multiple results
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Returns either an int or an error
Two results: the value and an error
One tuple result
explanation: Not a Result and not a tuple, just two return values; by convention the error is last and nil on success.

title: Error check
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Logs the error and keeps going
Panics and exits the program
Returns the error to the caller
explanation: This is what Rust's ? expands to; Go has no ?, so these three lines are written out every time.

title: Blank identifier
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Discards that result
A variable named underscore
A placeholder assigned later
explanation: Same as _ in Rust; Go refuses unused local variables, so unwanted results must go to _.

title: Struct literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Builds a map
Calls a function named User
Builds a User value by field name
explanation: Like a Rust struct literal but with colons; any field left out takes its zero value.

title: Case and visibility
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: An exported field, visible outside the package
An optional field
A private field, invisible outside the package
explanation: There is no pub: an uppercase first letter means exported, lowercase means package-private, for fields, functions and types alike.

title: Method receiver
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The receiver; u plays the role of self
The result type
The first ordinary parameter, a pointer
explanation: Methods are written outside the type with an explicitly named receiver; there is no self keyword. A pointer receiver is needed to modify fields.

title: Field through a pointer
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Changes u's field through the pointer
Does not compile; needs (*p).Name
Changes a copy of u
explanation: Field access through a pointer dereferences automatically: no -> and no (*p). This prints b.

title: Map lookup
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Looks up id; panics if it is missing
Looks up id; ok says if it exists
Looks up two keys at the same time
explanation: Map lookup does not return an Option: a missing key yields the zero value, and the second result tells you whether it was there.

title: make
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Creates a fixed-size array
Creates an empty, writable map
Declares the map type without allocating
explanation: A map must be made before writing; a declared but un-made map is nil, readable but panics on write.

title: if with a statement
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Two separate conditions, both must hold
Looks up first, then uses ok as the condition
Declares two package-level variables
explanation: An if may start with one statement; the condition follows the semicolon. It reads like if let Some(v) = cache.get(key).

title: Slice literal
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: A fixed-length array of 4
A set of 4 distinct values
A growable list with 4 elements
explanation: []T is a slice, the Vec<T> of Go; [4]int would be a fixed array, which is rarely used directly.

title: append
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Appends and keeps the returned slice
Builds a new array; the old slice is unchanged
Appends in place; the result can be dropped
explanation: append may reallocate, so it is always written s = append(s, x); dropping the result is a bug.

title: Slice expression
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: The element at index 3
A view of the first 3 elements
An independent copy of the first 3
explanation: Like &v[..3], a view that shares memory; modifying the result modifies items, and there is no borrow checker to warn you.

title: range loop
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Iterates: i is the index, item the element
Iterates the keys and values of a map
Iterates: i is the element, item the index
explanation: range yields the index and a copy of the element; to skip the index write for _, item := range items.

title: switch with several values
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Matches either value
Matches a two-element tuple
Runs two cases one after another
explanation: A case may list several values, like "paused" | "stopped"; every case breaks automatically, nothing falls through.

title: defer
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Unlocks when the function returns
Unlocks immediately
Unlocks on a background thread
explanation: There is no Drop; cleanup is done with defer, which runs when the enclosing function returns, last in first out.

title: goroutine
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Calls worker and waits for it to return
Declares a function named worker
Runs worker concurrently without waiting
explanation: The go keyword starts a goroutine, like thread::spawn but cheap; it returns no handle, so waiting is done with channels or a WaitGroup.

title: Channel send and receive
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Receives a value, waiting if none is ready
Sends a value, waiting for a receiver
Closes the channel
explanation: The arrow shows the data direction: ch <- v sends, <-ch receives; on an unbuffered channel both sides block until the other is ready.

title: Implicit interface
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Valid: having a String method is enough
Does not compile: User never declares Stringer
Converts User to a string and stores it in s
explanation: Interfaces are implemented implicitly: having the methods is all it takes, there is no impl Trait for. This is one of the biggest structural differences from Rust.

title: Formatting
question: What is the highlighted part?
choices: Builds and returns a string
Writes a line to the log file
Prints a line to standard output
explanation: Sprintf returns the string; Printf prints. %s is a string, %d an integer, %v prints anything.
